title: Jerusalem, 1099
hook: the First Crusade takes Jerusalem with great slaughter

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Muwatta, Malik's book, and the Maliki school his students carried west from Medina. Your line was: the school of medina traveled west.

A group of refugees reaches Baghdad in the month of Ramadan. They have come a long way, from Syria and from Jerusalem. A judge brings them into the caliph's court, and they tell what they saw. The chronicler Ibn al-Athir says their story brought tears to the eyes of those who heard it. Then he adds a line about the rulers: they were divided among themselves, and nothing was done. This part of the path turns to the Crusades, the Mongols and the Mamluks, and it starts with the city those refugees had fled: Jerusalem.
screen: `REFUGEES REACH BAGHDAD.` → `THE COURT WEEPS.` → `THE RULERS ARE DIVIDED.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem matters in Islam because of a journey. The Qur'an opens one of its surahs with it. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship the neighbourhood whereof We have blessed." Muslims understand the Far Distant Place of Worship, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, to be in Jerusalem, and tradition says believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the Ka'bah. So it was holy ground, shared in different ways with Jews and Christians, who hold it holy too. Armies from western Europe, the Franks of the First Crusade, marched a long way to take it. When the city fell, they killed a great many of the people inside. Muslim chroniclers like Ibn al-Athir describe killing in the Aqsa mosque itself, among scholars and devout people who had come to live near it. A chronicler of Damascus, Ibn al-Qalanisi, writes that Jews were burned in their synagogue. Chroniclers among the Franks recorded the killing too. Nobody's numbers can be trusted, so i won't give any. The Qur'an gives words for a moment of loss like this. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Those words are still said at news of a loss. Jerusalem, for a long time after, was a city in grief. And the refugees in Baghdad had named the problem the next generations would have to answer: a divided people.
screen: `THE NIGHT JOURNEY TO AL-AQSA.` · `HOLY GROUND, SHARED IN MANY WAYS.` · `THE CITY FALLS, THE KILLING BEGINS.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND UNTO HIM RETURNING.` · then, large: `A CITY IN GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the city that day, Muslims in the mosque, Jews in their synagogue, people of every faith in the streets, soldiers on every side; you don't need faces or numbers, just hold them all as people. If you pray, you can pray for all who died there with the words the Qur'an gives for loss: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we are God's, and to Him we return. If you don't pray, simply keep a silence for them.
Jerusalem. The city of the Night Journey and the Aqsa mosque, holy to Muslims, Jews and Christians, and the city taken with great slaughter in the First Crusade. Today's word.
Your line: a city in grief. Behind every count were people with names. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (we are God's, and to Him we return) at news of a death or loss, and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem is honored as the place of the Night Journey.

chat.says: Why is Jerusalem holy to Muslims, and not only to Jews and Christians?
options: The Night Journey reaches al-Aqsa there, and believers once prayed toward it.
Because the Prophet was born there before moving to Mecca and Medina.
Because the Ka'bah first stood there, before it was moved to Mecca.
chat.meaning: Qur'an 17:1 tells of the Night Journey to the Far Distant Place of Worship, which Muslims understand as al-Aqsa; tradition says believers once faced it.

notes: Start of the part 'Crusades, Mongols and Mamluks' (955–964).
The year in the title is not repeated in the spoken script; no casualty figures are given (Ibn al-Athir's figure is widely doubted). Confirm.
Ibn al-Athir's account of refugees reaching Baghdad in Ramadan, led by a qadi (al-Harawi), weeping in the diwan and breaking the fast: paraphrased; confirm details.
Ibn al-Qalanisi on Jews burned in the synagogue: confirm the source and wording.
'Chroniclers among the Franks recorded the killing too' (e.g. Gesta Francorum, Raymond of Aguilers): confirm, and that the framing is fair to Christian listeners.
Jerusalem as the first qibla and al-Aqsa as the site of the Night Journey: standard; confirm phrasing ('Muslims understand').
Practice invites prayer for all who died, of every faith; the Arabic is from Qur'an 2:156. Confirm.
Pickthall 17:1 and 2:156 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
